title: Leaving their beds
hookLine: they forsake their beds to call on their Lord in fear and hope (32:16)

cards: There's a particular quiet at about four in the morning. No traffic, no notifications. The fridge hums.
A bird tries one note and stops. Shift workers know it, new parents know it, and so do people who get up on purpose, before dawn, to pray.
Surah As-Sajdah, the Prostration, the thirty-second, is short, and one of its pictures of the believers is someone alone at night, getting out of a warm bed.

teach.h: THEIR SIDES DRAW AWAY FROM THEIR BEDS.
teach.b: The verse before describes those who, when reminded of God's signs, fall down in prostration; it's one of the places where readers traditionally prostrate as they recite, and the surah is named As-Sajdah.

Pickthall: "Who forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope". The Arabic is vivid: tatajafa junubuhum 'an al-madaji', their sides draw away from their beds, as if the body itself pulls back from sleep.
And the two words: fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. The night prayer holds both, honesty about what's wrong and reaching toward mercy.
The practice is called qiyam al-layl, standing in the night. Another name is tahajjud, from a root about sleep; the dictionaries give this form the sense of leaving it.
A hadith in Tirmidhi says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, explaining to Mu'adh ibn Jabal the doors of good, mentioned prayer in the middle of the night, then recited this very verse.

teach.h: THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.
teach.b: And a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that in the last third of every night, God descends to the nearest heaven and asks: who is calling on Me, that I may answer him? Who is asking of Me, that I may give him?

It's voluntary, not one of the five prayers: a few short units in the dark, as often or as rarely as someone chooses. Another hadith in Tirmidhi reports that the Prophet would not sleep until he had recited this surah.
The verse is honest about the cost, a warm bed and a little sleep, and about what it buys: time to call on God in fear and in hope.

how: Many Muslims pray tahajjud, voluntary night prayer, in the last part of the night before the dawn prayer, especially in Ramadan, and many recite Surah As-Sajdah before sleeping.

games.why: 32:16: their sides forsake their beds, and they call on their Lord in fear and hope.

practice: Picture tonight and, if it's safe and sensible for your sleep, an alarm a little before dawn, even fifteen minutes before you'd normally rise.

Picture the dark room, the cold floor, and one small thing done with that time: if you pray, two short units of prayer or a few words of your own; if you don't, a few minutes of stillness and gratitude.
Then back to sleep, or into the day.

wordCard.voice: Qiyam al-layl. Standing in the night: the voluntary prayer of people whose sides draw away from their beds, in fear and hope. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: standing in the night, the voluntary night prayer, also called tahajjud.

carryVoice: Your line: up in the night. Fear and hope can share the same dark hour. That's day five hundred thirty-seven.
